title: Transduction-Enabled Superconducting Quantum Repeater: Toward Deterministic Entanglement Distribution with High-Fidelity Gates
authors: Francesco Fiorini, Jing Wu, Andrew Cameron, Changqing Wang, Doga M. Kurkcuoglu, Rosario G. Garroppo, Michele Pagano, Silvia Zorzetti
abstract: Long-distance entanglement distribution is hindered by photon loss in optical fibers and the nocloning theorem. Optical quantum repeater (QR) protocols rely on Bell state measurements (BSMs), they are intrinsically limited to probabilistic photon operations and fail 50% of the time. We propose a hybrid approach to building quantum repeaters that combines the high transmission speed of photonic qubits in optical fiber with the high-fidelity quantum processing capabilities enabled by superconducting circuits. The transduction-enabled superconducting QR (TESQR) architecture eliminates the need for probabilistic BSMs and allows deterministic processing operations. The TESQR framework always yields a final state at the remote nodes rather than aborting on photon loss, manifesting deterministic entanglement distribution within certain parameter regimes. We evaluate the performance by assessing output-state fidelities and success probabilities of entanglement distribution using realistic noise models. Additionally, we integrate an entanglement purification scheme and evaluate the performance through numerical simulations in QuTiP environment. Our results show that, for entanglement swapping, the proposed scheme improves the entanglement distribution rate by an average of 63% and by up to 159% compared with photonic-only architectures. Moreover, after purification, the end-to-end fidelities exceed 0.8 over distances up to 20 km.
summary: This paper introduces the Transduction-Enabled Superconducting Quantum Repeater (TESQR) to overcome the probabilistic limitations of current quantum repeaters. By integrating superconducting circuits to perform deterministic entanglement swapping, the scheme significantly boosts entanglement distribution rates and maintains high fidelity over practical distances. It represents a crucial step toward building scalable quantum communication networks.
main_problem: Long-distance entanglement distribution is limited by photon loss and the probabilistic nature of Bell State Measurements (BSMs) in traditional quantum repeaters.
main_result: The proposed Transduction-Enabled Superconducting Quantum Repeater (TESQR) improves entanglement distribution rates by up to 159% and achieves end-to-end fidelities exceeding 0.8 over 20 km after purification.
method: The authors propose a hybrid architecture combining photonic qubits with superconducting circuits to enable deterministic entanglement processing, avoiding probabilistic BSMs.
model_or_system: The system integrates three components at the repeater node: quantum transduction (optical to microwave), coupling to a superconducting QPU, and local entanglement swapping performed via microwave gates. The analysis uses quantum channel formalism and density matrix evolution.
key_observables: Output-state fidelities, success probabilities of entanglement distribution, and end-to-end fidelities.
important_parameters: Fiber length (up to 20 km), transduction efficiency ($\eta_t$), coupling efficiencies ($\eta_{ph}, \eta_{qb}$), and gate error rates.
main_assumptions: Ideal memory performance is assumed, and the analysis initially focuses on quantum-processing performance metrics rather than resource costs.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the TESQR node architecture (Transduction $ightarrow$ Coupling $ightarrow$ Superconducting QPU). Other figures analyze the degradation of fidelity due to asymmetries in transduction efficiency, fiber length, and thermal noise.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of current quantum repeaters, then details the TESQR architecture, models the state evolution through sequential steps (Source $ightarrow$ Transmission $ightarrow$ Transduction $ightarrow$ Coupling $ightarrow$ Swapping), and finally analyzes the performance under various noise and asymmetry conditions.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of scaling quantum networks by proposing a concrete, high-fidelity physical implementation that bridges the gap between long-haul photonics and solid-state quantum computation.
